18.0.s.en: (1) The reign of Hezekiah and his reforms

18.0.0.en: Hezekiah became king over Judah at the age of twenty-five, and that was in the third year of Hoshea the son of Elah king of Israel, and he reigned in Jerusalem, and his reign lasted twenty-nine years. His mother’s name was Abi, the daughter of Zechariah.

18.0.1.en: Hezekiah began to reign in the third year of Hoshea, that is, the fifteenth year of the reign of his father Ahaz; for it is mentioned that Hoshea began to reign in the twelfth year of Ahaz (ch. 17:1), although it is mentioned in (ch. 16:2) that Ahaz reigned sixteen years. The difference of a year between fifteen and sixteen is because parts of a year are sometimes counted and sometimes not counted. This is the time of Hezekiah’s reigning alone, after the death of his father Ahaz, but he had reigned a period with him before his death, as was the custom of some kings in this time, to prepare their sons for the kingship. And it is beautiful that Hezekiah, despite his living with his wicked father Ahaz, did not imitate him in his evil but quietly held fast to the commandments of God until he reigned alone and had the authority, and then his goodness and his spiritual reforms appeared, and he was obedient to the commands of God which he heard from Isaiah the prophet, whereas his father neglected the words of Isaiah.

18.1.0.en: His works were good, and he followed in the footsteps of his great forefather David in his righteousness. It is not said of the kings of Judah that they were good and perfect like David, except of three, the first of whom is Asa (1 Kgs 15:11), then Hezekiah, and in the end Josiah (2 Kgs 22:1, 2). The brilliance of these three appears in that they were righteous, although their fathers were wicked.

18.1.1.en: And we find that it was said of these three that they did what was right like David their father; this is true repentance, that is, returning to the right position in the relationship with God. David represents the pure relationship to which a person should return when he repents, so that he becomes completely upright in the eyes of the Lord, and not merely partially upright, as we mentioned of some of the kings before Hezekiah in the series of the kings of Judah, such as Jotham, Uzziah and Amaziah.

18.2.0.en: Nehushtan: a Hebrew word meaning a piece of bronze.

18.2.1.en: The Second Book of Chronicles tells us (2 Chr 29) that Hezekiah opened the house of the Lord and began to organize the worship in it and called the people to keep the Passover, and they returned to God. And Hezekiah removed the places of pagan worship on the hills and broke the images and cut down the poles and crushed the bronze serpent that Moses had made, because the children of Israel had burned incense to it, and they had called it Nehushtan.

18.2.2.en: God had commanded Moses to make this bronze serpent so that everyone bitten by the serpents might look at it and be healed (Num 21:8), and the children of Israel kept it because it signified a blessing. But when they sank low and worshiped idols, they considered this serpent an idol and worshiped it.

18.2.3.en: This shows the courage of Hezekiah and his holding fast to God, in that he did not fear the rebellion of the people, many of whom had become attached to the worship of idols in the days of his father, and he did not fear the king of Assyria either, who had commanded the spread of the worship of the idols of Assyria in Judah and in all the kingdom of Assyria; for it is said of Hezekiah that he “removed,” and he did not wait for the repentance of the people and their support of him, but removed the evil himself, and then the people returned to God and followed Hezekiah. He is thus a man of initiative and strong in his holding fast to God and his removal of evil.

18.2.4.en: We also notice how Satan was able to turn the bronze serpent, which signified the work and blessing of God, into an idol that the people worshiped when they drew away from God; for Satan is always crafty and deceitful and exploits a person’s distance from God to humiliate him.

18.3.0.en: Hezekiah relied on the power of God, and among the former kings of Israel there was none like him in his trust in God.

18.3.1.en: Your trust in God gives you tranquility and opens to you the doors of relationship and the sense of God and, consequently, righteous conduct, and so you also become an example to those around you.

18.4.0.en: He clave to the Lord and did not turn aside from His ways, but lived as the commandments required, which the Lord commanded Moses.

18.4.1.en: And we notice in (vv. 5, 6) that it was said of Hezekiah that he trusted in God and clave to Him and kept His commandments; for whoever believes in God and trusts in Him loves Him and clings to Him in prayers and readings of His word in the Holy Bible, and so he can easily keep His commandments and always strive to carry them out. Therefore believe in God, and you will love Him, and then you will keep His commandments.

18.5.0.en: Because of Hezekiah’s trust in the Lord and his removal of the worship of idols and his concern for the worship of God, God supported him in all his works, and he prospered in them, and in this Hezekiah rebelled against the king of Assyria and the worship of his idols. But Assyria did not attack him, because it was occupied with wars in other countries. God rejoiced in the uprightness of Hezekiah, but the people agreed with him, though not with all their heart, as shown by the fact that Isaiah, who was his contemporary, did not cease to rebuke them, because he knew the evil of their hearts, as appears from the whole prophecy of Isaiah.

18.6.0.en: From the tower of the watchmen to the fenced city: from the small farm to the large fortified city.

18.6.1.en: It seems that the king of Assyria had given some cities of Judah to the king of Gaza, and so Hezekiah fought the Philistines in their city Gaza and smote them and recovered the cities that had been seized from Judah. And God was with him, and he defeated the Philistines in their fortified cities and in their small unwalled villages.

18.6.2.en: We notice that Hezekiah’s rebellion against Assyria did not anger God, as shown by God’s support of Hezekiah against the Philistines, and then against Assyria, when He killed its armies by means of the king, as we shall see. But God was angry with Zedekiah, the last of the kings of Judah, because he did not obey Jeremiah the prophet, who told him to submit to Babylon, because it was a divine chastening and God had commanded this chastening (ch. 25:5-7).

18.7.0.en: In the fourth year of King Hezekiah king of Judah, which corresponds to the seventh year of King Hoshea the son of Elah king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria threatened Samaria and his armies besieged it.

18.8.0.en: The siege lasted three years, after which the city surrendered and the king of Assyria occupied it. That was in the sixth year of Hezekiah, which corresponds to the ninth year of Hoshea.

18.9.0.en: The king of Assyria carried the children of Israel captive and led them to Assyria and settled them in the cities subject to his authority, which are Halah and Habor by the river of Gozan, and also in the cities of the Medes (see the previous chapter for the identification of those cities).

18.10.0.en: This severe blow to the people of Israel was a chastening for them from the Lord, because they had stopped their ears to His warnings and broken His covenant, and all that Moses commanded them they did not heed and did not do, but worshiped idols and followed their evil lusts and provoked God.

18.10.1.en: It is clear that Hezekiah benefited from the captivity of Israel and their bondage, for he increased in his clinging to God and in his removal of pagan forms of worship.

18.10.2.en: Learn from the errors of others so that you guard against them, and so keep away from the sources of evil and fear God and worship Him, and you will live in tranquility and peace and God will prosper you in your works.

18.11.s.en: (3) Assyria takes the cities of Judah and takes tribute

18.11.0.en: After the final destruction of Israel by Shalmaneser king of Assyria, his successor Sennacherib attacked all the fortified cities of Judah and took them. That was in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah.

18.12.0.en: Lachish: a fortified city in the kingdom of Judah, lying west of Hebron, fifteen miles away.

18.12.1.en: A talent of silver: it has several weights ranging between 20 and 40 kg.

18.12.2.en: A talent of gold: equal to 17.4 kg.

18.12.3.en: Despite the uprightness of Hezekiah’s heart, his faith was shaken when he found that Sennacherib king of Assyria had taken the fortified cities of Judah. Consequently there remained before him only the taking of Jerusalem, and he feared the Assyrian attack and did not rely on God, so he sent to Sennacherib to apologize to him for not submitting to him and to beg him to leave the cities of Judah, in return for paying him the tribute that he would fix. So Sennacherib fixed a heavy tribute on Hezekiah, three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold. But sadly Sennacherib betrayed the agreement and attacked Jerusalem afterward, and these are the characteristics of the wicked. This was so that Hezekiah might learn to rely on God alone and not make agreements with the wicked.

18.12.4.en: Be loving to all people, but do not arrange your life on the basis of your relationship with the wicked. Keep away from them and pray for them with love and deal with them in a limited way and rely on God, and He will protect you from them. Be ready to help them if they are in need, but do not trust them nor rely on them.

18.13.0.en: The tribute was very great, and so Hezekiah was compelled to take all the silver found in the treasury of the house of the Lord.

18.14.0.en: In order to pay the gold that he owed, Hezekiah did not find enough in his treasuries or the treasuries of the house of the Lord, and so he was compelled to strip the gold from the doors and the pillars of the house of the Lord and send it to Sennacherib.

18.15.0.en: The conduit of the upper pool, which is in the highway of the fuller’s field: a conduit lying outside the walls of Jerusalem and beside them and reaching inside the walls to a pool inside the city, to supply the city with water; this conduit is beside the fuller’s field, the fuller being one who whitens cloth. They say that there was a statue of this fuller until the seventh century, and this conduit lies north of the city of Jerusalem.

18.15.1.en: Sennacherib betrayed the agreement with Hezekiah, for after taking the very great tribute he also attacked Jerusalem with a great army and sent two of the commanders of his army, and the third, the king’s cupbearer and his spokesman, because he spoke Hebrew well, to King Hezekiah, demanding that he surrender the city and not rely on his God.

18.16.1.en: When the men of Sennacherib called to King Hezekiah from outside the walls, he sent out to them three of the officers who assisted him, and they stood on the wall to confer with the commanders of the army of Sennacherib.

18.17.0.en: Vain words: that is, you have no power but words with which to defend yourself in war.

18.17.1.en: Strength for the war: power with which to fight.

18.17.2.en: Rabshakeh, the official spokesman in the name of King Sennacherib, spoke, addressing the men of Hezekiah who stood on the wall, to deliver to him the message of Sennacherib, who rebuked Hezekiah, declaring to him his weakness, for he had nothing but mere words. How can he rely on words and rebel against the great king of Assyria, the conqueror of all the kingdoms of the earth?

18.17.3.en: From this the pride of Sennacherib and his men appears, and their contempt for God and His children and His city Jerusalem. For they regard the faith of Hezekiah and his people as mere words, resting on nothing, because they do not believe in the power of God.

18.17.4.en: Do not be troubled by the threats of the wicked, for they do not know the power of your God, who protects you; you are stronger with God than all their power and authority. Stand firm in your faith and principles, and you will see with your own eyes their shaking, for they are mere words without power, and Satan and his followers are nothing before the power of God, on whom you rely.

18.18.0.en: A bruised reed: a stick of cane that has been struck and is almost broken.

18.18.1.en: Sennacherib rebuked Hezekiah, thinking that he had relied on Egypt and for this reason rebelled against Assyria, although this had not happened, because Hezekiah relied on God and not on men.

18.18.2.en: And he likened Egypt, in mockery, to a bruised reed, that is, very weak, so that if someone leans on it, it does not support him, but because it is weak and has been struck, it will break and pierce his palm and wound it and pierce his hand. By this he means that relying on Egypt will harm everyone who relies on it, and this confirms the king of Assyria’s immersion in pride.

18.19.0.en: Continuing his casting of doubt on Hezekiah’s strength, Sennacherib said to him, if you have not relied on Egypt but have relied on God, know that God is angry with you, because you have broken down His altars. For Sennacherib, as a pagan king, does not know the difference between the temples of the idols, which Hezekiah removed, and the altar of God, which is in His Temple, and so he said to Hezekiah that you have removed the altars of God and left one altar, and of course this angers Him and He will not support you against me. Sennacherib feels that what Hezekiah says, in his reliance on God, is deceit, because as a pagan who believes in a plurality of gods, how can one tear down the altars of the gods and yet rely on them? He does not believe in the one God, who rejects foreign gods. But all the words of Sennacherib were a war of doubt from Satan, before which Hezekiah, who believed in God, was not shaken.

18.19.1.en: And we notice that the unfaithfulness of the Jews, in their worship of idols on the high places and their setting up of poles, is what made Sennacherib stumble and caused him to blaspheme God.

18.19.2.en: The strange thing is that Sennacherib casts all these doubts and forgot what had happened to the inhabitants of Samaria, which Assyria took and settled many Gentiles in, and the lions devoured them, and he commanded that a priest of the children of Israel be sent to teach them how to please the god of the land, because he is a mighty god; if he is mighty, why does he cast doubt on him? And why does he not submit to him? But it is the pride of man that leads him to destruction. And this is what actually happened with Sennacherib and all his army, as we shall see in the coming events.

18.20.0.en: And Sennacherib offered a third doubt to Hezekiah about his strength, for he said to him that you have no horsemen to fight, and indeed made an offer to mock him and said to him, I will give you two thousand horses, if you can find two thousand riders to ride upon them, and of course you do not have them, so you are weak and cannot stand before me; surrender and hand over the city.

18.21.0.en: So how can you stand against a single one of the least of the commanders of the king of Assyria, relying on Egypt to supply you with war chariots and horsemen?

18.22.0.en: A fourth doubt is offered by Rabshakeh on behalf of Sennacherib, and he says: And now, do you think that I have come up to destroy this place of my own accord? The Lord is the One who sent me and charged me with laying waste these lands; he lies and claims that God sent him, although Satan is the one who moves him.

18.22.1.en: Do not believe the doubts of Satan that he sends to you through the mouth of the wicked, or by thoughts within you, for he is a liar and the father of lies. Be sure that all the logical arguments he offers are a false interpretation from himself, as shown by the fact that you are troubled by his words and that his thoughts are all destructive. Drive out his thoughts quickly and seek God and be sure that He is able to protect you from them, however great your weakness.

18.23.0.en: The deputies of Hezekiah feared the effect of the words of the commanders of the king of Assyria on the morale of their soldiers, and so they asked Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic, which the three deputies of Hezekiah understand, and not to speak in Hebrew, lest the soldiers stationed on the wall and all the people hear and be afraid. Aramaic is the language spoken by the Assyrians and understood by the educated among the Jews, such as the deputies of Hezekiah, while the rest of the Jews know only Hebrew.

18.24.0.en: Their own dung: their waste, that is, their excrement.

18.24.1.en: Rabshakeh rejected the request of the deputies of Hezekiah and declared the truth of this dialogue, that its aim was not to come to an understanding with Hezekiah but to cast doubt on the soldiers and people of God, so that they would fall into despair and surrender; for the Assyrians would besiege the city until those in it fell into hunger and severe thirst and were compelled to eat their own waste and drink their own urine. And so he began to speak with strong threats and not mere doubts, declaring that if they did not surrender they would certainly die of hunger and thirst.

18.25.0.en: Rabshakeh continued his challenge to the deputies of Hezekiah, and cried with a loud voice in the Hebrew language, directing his words to the soldiers of Judah, calling them to listen to the message of Assyria to them, and he said:

18.26.0.en: Thus says the king: Do not be deceived by what Hezekiah tries to persuade you of, for he is not able to deliver you out of the hand of the king of Assyria.

18.27.0.en: And let not Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the Lord, saying that He will deliver you, so that you do not fall into the hand of the king of Assyria; God is unable to deliver you, and Sennacherib will storm your city.

18.28.1.en: Do not listen to him nor believe what he says. Here is the king of Assyria offering you a generous offer, that you declare your surrender to him, and then you will move about freely and live in peace, and every one of you will eat of his own vine and of his fig tree and drink the waters of his own cistern. So after trying to make them doubt, he offers them false happiness and lying promises.

18.28.2.en: These are the very words of Satan, which he always speaks in the hearts of people, promising them to provide all the means of happiness; woe to the one who listens to him. Is this not what happened with our first parents? And here Sennacherib demands that they come out of Jerusalem, as Satan demands that we come out of the Church and plunge into the lusts of the world to find happiness, though in truth he will enslave us and humble us.

18.29.0.en: Sennacherib continues to deceive the inhabitants of Jerusalem, promising them that he will move them to a fertile land, to enjoy a better life, instead of dying if they obey Hezekiah and do not surrender. The truth is that he will enslave them and move them from their land and scatter them throughout the regions of his kingdom and humble them. Yet whoever examines the words of Sennacherib knows that he is deceitful, for he says that he will move them to a land like their own land, so why should they lose their fertile land? They live in safety under the care of their God. The solution is steadfastness in faith in God, and then the falseness of all the doubts and promises of Sennacherib appears.

18.30.0.en: Was any of the gods of the nations, whose lands the army of the king of Assyria invaded, ever able to repel the king of Assyria? The answer to this is that the gods of the nations are not gods, but God alone is able to protect His people.

18.31.0.en: Hena: the town of Anah on the river Euphrates.

18.31.1.en: Arpad: a city in Aram whose site today is “Tell Arfad,” at a distance of twenty kilometers north of Hamath.

18.31.2.en: The Jews who dwelt in the kingdom of Israel, that is, the cities of Samaria, worshiped pagan gods whom Sennacherib mentions here, and Sennacherib thought that these gods had not been able to protect the cities of Samaria because he is stronger than they, and forgot that God, whom the inhabitants of the cities of Samaria had left, was the One who was angry with them for their worship of foreign gods, and so allowed him to attack them and occupy their land. And once more the unfaithfulness of the people of God in the cities of Samaria appears, by their worship of idols, for they caused Sennacherib to blaspheme God and consider Him a weak god, among the gods, unable to resist him.

18.32.0.en: Sennacherib considered God merely one god among the gods, and since all the gods of the nations had been unable to protect their peoples, the God of Israel is therefore unable to protect Jerusalem.

18.33.0.en: None of the soldiers of Judah answered what the commanders of the king of Assyria said; for King Hezekiah had given instructions to everyone to be silent and not to answer the king of Assyria and his commanders anything, lest the effect of doubt on the people increase. And argument with the wicked falls into many sins, for the best thing to do with the thoughts of Satan is to drive them out and not discuss them. This shows the awe in which Hezekiah was held; because he was righteous and feared God, his people respected him and obeyed him and trusted his word.

18.34.0.en: The king’s deputies returned with their clothes rent, in grief at what they had heard, and told King Hezekiah what had been said, for they could not bear the blasphemy of King Sennacherib against God and his casting of doubts on the people.
